title: Nahum 1:1–8
context: Nahum the Elkoshite sets down a vision, a revelation about Nineveh. The prophet proclaims the LORD as a jealous God who avenges, slow to anger and great in power, who will by no means leave the guilty unpunished, and who has his way in the whirlwind and the storm. The sea and the rivers, Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon are pictured as withering at his rebuke; mountains quake, hills melt, and the earth trembles at his presence. No one can stand before his indignation, yet the LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble, and he knows those who take refuge in him. With an overflowing flood he will make a full end of her place and pursue his enemies into darkness. The confession that the LORD is slow to anger and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished echoes Exodus 34:6–7, the same creed Jonah 4:2 applies to Nineveh’s being spared; this book announces judgment on the same city, and the two accounts are named without being merged. Many readers notice a partial alphabetic pattern in verses 2–8, a beginning of an acrostic that is not carried through in a complete or regular way; the WEB text does not mark any letters. The location of Elkosh is not given in the heading.

verses.text: A revelation about Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.
verses.arminianNotes:
“A revelation about Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.” The book is named as a vision and as a revelation about Nineveh, the Assyrian city. The prophet is Nahum the Elkoshite; the heading does not locate Elkosh. Jonah earlier told of Nineveh’s being spared; this book announces judgment on the same city, and the two accounts are not merged.

Arminian readers take the heading as a real word given to Nahum, a vision about a named city that will now hear the LORD’s case against it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same heading as the LORD’s appointed revelation, a vision whose subject is Nineveh from the first line.

Shared ground: the book is Nahum’s vision, and its subject is Nineveh. The traditions begin together.

verses.text: The LORD is a jealous God and avenges. The LORD avenges and is full of wrath. The LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries, and he maintains wrath against his enemies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD is a jealous God and avenges. The LORD avenges and is full of wrath. The LORD takes vengeance on his adversaries, and he maintains wrath against his enemies.” The opening confession is about the LORD’s character: jealousy, vengeance, and wrath against adversaries and enemies. The words are heavy, and they are a statement of who he is, not a scene of violence.

Arminian readers hear a holy jealousy for his name and his people, a real wrath against enemies, and a God whose vengeance is just, not capricious, a word Nineveh can still recognize as a warning.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same jealousy, vengeance, and maintained wrath as the LORD’s own settled character, the ground of the judgment the book will announce.

Shared ground: the LORD is jealous and avenges, and he maintains wrath against his enemies. The character sketch opens the vision.

verses.text: The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. The LORD has his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will by no means leave the guilty unpunished. The LORD has his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.” Slowness to anger and greatness in power stand together, and the guilty will not go unpunished. The storm language is the LORD’s way in the world, clouds as the dust of his feet.

Arminian readers hear patience that is real, a slowness to anger that does not cancel the word that the guilty will not be left unpunished, and a power that still leaves room for the warning to be heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the slowness to anger, the greatness in power, and the refusal to leave the guilty unpunished as the LORD’s own consistent character, already at work in the storm he rules.

Shared ground: he is slow to anger and will not leave the guilty unpunished. Both lines belong to the same confession.

verses.text: He rebukes the sea and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan and Carmel languish. The flower of Lebanon languishes.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD rebukes the sea and makes it dry, and dries up all the rivers. Bashan and Carmel languish, and the flower of Lebanon languishes. The creation language recalls a God who can dry the sea, and the proud green places of the north fail at his rebuke. The verse is a picture of his power over land and water, not a campaign report.

Arminian readers hear a rebuke that reaches sea and river and the flowering hills, a power meant to humble the proud and to warn a city that has trusted its own waters and walls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the dried sea and rivers, and the languishing of Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon, as the LORD’s own act, the same power that will reach Nineveh.

Shared ground: sea, rivers, and the green heights fail at his rebuke. The verse is cosmic in scope, and it stays in those images.

verses.text: The mountains quake before him, and the hills melt away. The earth trembles at his presence, yes, the world, and all who dwell in it.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The mountains quake before him, and the hills melt away. The earth trembles at his presence, yes, the world, and all who dwell in it.” The quaking is before him, and the whole earth, with all who dwell in it, trembles at his presence. The language is theophany: the world itself is not steady when he is near.

Arminian readers hear a presence that the world cannot ignore, a trembling that still calls every dweller to take the warning seriously, not only the city named in the heading.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the quaking mountains, the melting hills, and the trembling of the earth and its dwellers as the LORD’s own presence made known.

Shared ground: the earth trembles at his presence. The word reaches beyond Nineveh to the world that dwells on the earth.

verses.text: Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the fierceness of his anger? His wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken apart by him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Who can stand before his indignation? Who can endure the fierceness of his anger?” The wrath is poured out like fire, and the rocks are broken apart by him. The questions expect no standing and no enduring. Wrath like fire and rocks broken apart tell the fierceness of his anger, still in the language of the storm and the mountain, not as a scene to be enlarged.

Arminian readers hear a question that still searches the hearer: who can stand? The answer is that no one endures this anger in their own strength, a call to refuge that the next verse will name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the unanswerable questions, the wrath poured out like fire, and the rocks broken apart as the LORD’s own indignation, before which no adversary can stand.

Shared ground: no one can stand before his indignation, and the rocks break at his anger. The next verse will set goodness and refuge beside this fierceness.

verses.text: The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; and he knows those who take refuge in him.” Goodness, a stronghold, and knowledge of those who take refuge stand immediately after the unendurable anger. The refuge is real, and it is in him.

Arminian readers hear a genuine invitation in the stronghold and the taking of refuge, a goodness that is there to be trusted in the day of trouble, and a knowing that answers those who actually come to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the LORD’s goodness, the stronghold, and his knowing of those who take refuge in him as his own faithful care of his people, sure in the day of trouble.

Shared ground: the LORD is good, and he is a stronghold. The LORD knows those who take refuge in him, and that line is a comfort, not a new dispute.

verses.text: But with an overflowing flood, he will make a full end of her place, and will pursue his enemies into darkness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But with an overflowing flood, he will make a full end of her place, and will pursue his enemies into darkness.” The “but” turns from the stronghold to the city: an overflowing flood, a full end of her place, enemies pursued into darkness. “her place” is heard as Nineveh’s, the city already named. The flood is the oracle’s image for a complete end, and it is not turned into a later siege report.

Arminian readers hear a full end that is still announced as a warning, a flood that will overtake the city’s place, and a darkness into which enemies are pursued, a word Nineveh can still take as the LORD’s sentence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the overflowing flood, the full end of her place, and the pursuit of enemies into darkness as the LORD’s own appointed judgment on the city.

Shared ground: he will make a full end of her place. The stronghold of verse 7 and the flood of verse 8 stand in one confession.
